name: Kurt Hamrin
milestone_by_age_26: Top scorer of the Swedish Allsvenskan in the 1954-55 season with 22 goals for AIK at age 20, establishing himself as one of Sweden's most promising footballers before transferring to Juventus at 21.
early_history_summary: Hamrin grew up in Stockholm and played youth football for Huvudsta IS, Råsunda IS, and AIK. He made his senior debut for AIK in 1952 at age 17 and became the Swedish league's top scorer in 1954-55 with 22 goals, earning a transfer to Juventus in 1956.
family_context_summary: Born the fifth son of a house painter in Stockholm; worked as a teenager in the print room of Dagens Nyheter newspaper while playing football, as the Swedish league was still amateur.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; father was a house painter with no known football connection.
primary_early_advantage_tags: AIK youth system, Swedish football culture, early senior debut, working-class background
evidence_summary: Hamrin was the fifth son of a house painter in Stockholm and worked at a newspaper print room while playing amateur football. He joined AIK's youth system at 15, made his senior debut at 17, and became the league's top scorer at 20 with 22 goals. The Swedish football culture and AIK's platform provided early exposure, but his working-class background meant he had to work another job. His rapid rise to top scorer demonstrates exceptional physical talent and early domain immersion.
starting_point: Born in Stockholm, Sweden in 1934, the fifth son of a house painter; worked as a teenager in a newspaper print room while playing amateur football.

He won the men's singles at the 6th National Games in 1987 and was selected for the Chinese national team in 1988, going on to win multiple World Championship and Olympic gold medals.
family_context_summary: Born into a family of musicians in Beijing; father was a composer and mother a national first-class singer. His father initially had him learn violin but switched to table tennis due to his short fingers.

milestone_by_age_26: Won the FIVB World Championship gold medal with Poland in 1974 at age 21, followed by Olympic gold at the 1976 Montreal Olympics at age 23, as part of Poland's golden era of volleyball.

He joined the Polish junior team at 18, winning European Junior Vice-Champion in 1972, and became a key member of the senior national team from 1973, winning World Championship gold in 1974 and Olympic gold in 1976.
family_context_summary: Born in Lublin, Poland; father Kazimierz was a volleyball player who became his first coach, and brother Wojciech also played volleyball at Avia Świdnik.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a volleyball player and his first coach; brother also played volleyball, creating a family volleyball environment at Avia Świdnik.

His brother also played, creating a family volleyball environment. He was described as a natural talent who was guided by his father and then by national junior team coach Władysław Pałaszewski. He entered the Polish national team pipeline at 18 and became a key player in Poland's golden era, winning World Championship gold at 21 and Olympic gold at 23. His 197cm height and natural athleticism were significant physical advantages.

She won the Romanian national championship at 18 in 1964, transferred to CSA Steaua in Bucharest, and won the Junior World Championships in 1965.

She transferred to CSA Steaua Bucharest, an elite military sports club that served as a major fencing pipeline. She won the Junior World Championships at 19 and earned individual bronze at the 1966 World Championships. Training alongside future world-class fencers like Ileana Gyulai and József Szepessy provided a high-quality peer environment. Her Hungarian minority status in Transylvania may have created outsider motivation.

name: Jaromír Jágr
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Stanley Cup with the Pittsburgh Penguins in 1991 at age 19 as an NHL rookie, followed by a second consecutive Stanley Cup in 1992 at age 20, after being drafted 5th overall in the 1990 NHL Entry Draft at age 18.
early_history_summary: Jágr began skating at age 3 in Kladno, Czechoslovakia, and attended a specialized hockey school. He played with older children from age 10, debuted professionally for Poldi SONP Kladno at 15, and became the youngest member of the Czechoslovakia national team at 17. Drafted 5th overall by Pittsburgh in 1990, he joined the NHL immediately and won the Stanley Cup in his rookie season.
family_context_summary: Born in Kladno, Czechoslovakia, and lived on a farm with his parents and sister. His father had him do intensive physical training including 1,000 squats daily and running laps alongside a tractor from a young age.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was not a hockey player but provided intensive physical conditioning training from childhood; the family lived on a farm in Kladno, a town with a strong hockey tradition.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kladno hockey school, Czechoslovak hockey system, father physical training, early pro debut at 15, Mario Lemieux mentorship, NHL at 18
evidence_summary: Jágr was a prodigy who began skating at 3 in Kladno, a Czech hockey powerhouse. His father provided intensive physical conditioning from childhood, including 1,000 daily squats that built his legendary leg strength. He attended a specialized hockey school, played with older children at 10, turned professional at 15, and was the youngest Czechoslovak national team member at 17. Drafted 5th overall by Pittsburgh in 1990, he won the Stanley Cup as an 18-year-old rookie, mentored by Mario Lemieux. The combination of Czechoslovakia's elite hockey pipeline, his father's training, and his extraordinary physical talent created a rare trajectory.

name: Ljubomir Ljubojević
milestone_by_age_26: Awarded the FIDE Grandmaster title in 1971 at age 21, following his U-20 vice-world championship in 1969/70 at age 19 and International Master title in 1970, making him one of the youngest grandmasters of his era.
early_history_summary: Born in Titovo Užice, Yugoslavia, Ljubojević was taught chess by his father, a merchant navy officer. He emerged on the international scene in the late 1960s, winning the World Student Team Championship with Yugoslavia in 1969 and becoming U-20 vice-world champion in Groningen. He was awarded the IM title in 1970 and the GM title in 1971, then won the tournament at Palma de Mallorca in 1971.
family_context_summary: Born in Titovo Užice, Yugoslavia; father was a merchant navy officer who taught him chess. The family admired Mikhail Tal, which influenced Ljubojević's aggressive playing style.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a merchant navy officer who taught his son chess; not a chess professional but provided early introduction and inspiration through admiration of Mikhail Tal.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Yugoslav chess boom, father taught chess, Tal influence, Interzonal in Portoroz 1958, chess culture
evidence_summary: Ljubojević was taught chess by his father, a merchant navy officer, in Titovo Užice, Yugoslavia. He benefited from Yugoslavia's remarkable chess boom in the late 1950s, triggered by the Interzonal Tournament in Portorož 1958 and the Candidates Tournament in Bled 1959, which created a national chess culture. Mikhail Tal's style deeply influenced his aggressive play. He won the World Student Team Championship at 18, became U-20 vice-world champion at 19, IM at 19-20, and GM at 20-21. He paid his own way to the 1970 Siegen Olympiad to play blitz against the world's best, demonstrating exceptional initiative and domain immersion.
starting_point: Born in Titovo Užice, Yugoslavia in 1950; father was a merchant navy officer who taught him chess; family admired Mikhail Tal, influencing his aggressive playing style.
current_position: Retired Serbian chess grandmaster living in Spain; FIDE rating 2571 as of 2025; peaked at world No. 3 in 1983.
